0.title: Last Words: The Final Letter of the Apostle Paul
0.overview:
There is a letter that reads like a last will and testament, a soldier’s final dispatch from the front, and a father’s farewell to his son — all at once. Paul writes 2 Timothy from a Roman dungeon, by tradition the Mamertine Prison below the Capitoline Hill, where prisoners awaited execution. He has already stood before Nero’s tribunal; he expects to stand there again, and this time he does not expect to survive. He has been abandoned by most of his colleagues. Demas has gone back to the world. The churches of Asia have turned away. The winter is coming and he has no cloak. Only Luke is with him.

And yet the letter is not a cry of despair but an act of faith. Paul is not finished. He is fighting, praying, thinking, teaching to the last. He writes to Timothy — the son of his heart, the young man he circumcised and took on mission, who is now in Ephesus struggling with false teachers and the creeping temptation to soft-pedal the gospel for the sake of peace — and he writes with the urgency of a man who knows the window is closing. Guard the deposit. Don’t be ashamed. Endure suffering. Preach the word. These are not polite suggestions; they are dying instructions.

The letter is the most personal in the Pauline corpus. More than anywhere else we see Paul the man: Paul who remembers Timothy’s tears and longs to see him, who is comforted by Onesiphorus’s courage, who feels the sting of Alexander’s opposition, who in his final lines sends greetings from people whose names he has not forgotten. The great apostle is a human being who is cold, lonely, and facing death — and whose faith in the Jesus who appears in this letter (“remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead”) is, in the end, the only thing that has not shaken.

Is this really Paul’s last letter? Acts ends with Paul alive in Rome after two years under guard (Acts 28:30). The early church believed he was released, travelled again, and was arrested a second time under Nero, and this letter fits that setting: he has had a first defense (4:16), he expects to die (4:6), and he writes from harsher chains than in Acts. It was probably written around AD 64–67, shortly before his execution.

The letter is addressed to the minister, but it speaks to every Christian who must hold something precious in a world that does not want it. The deposit Paul entrusts to Timothy — the gospel of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen — is the same deposit entrusted to every generation of the church. Guard it. Pass it on. It is worth dying for. Paul’s life proves the claim.

1.title: Guard the Deposit: Courage, the Gospel, and Faithful Examples
1.overview:
These are Paul’s last written words. He is in prison in Rome and expects to die (4:6). He writes to Timothy, his beloved son in the faith, who is gifted, sincere and timid. Paul remembers his tears and his believing mother and grandmother, and then presses the charge: rekindle God’s gift, for God gave not a spirit of fear but of power, love and self-control. Do not be ashamed of the gospel or of me; share in suffering by God’s power.

The ground of courage is the gospel itself (vv. 9–10): God saved us by his own purpose and grace, given in Christ before time began, and Christ has abolished death. So Paul can say, “I know whom I have believed.” The chapter ends with a choice of examples: all Asia, which turned away, and Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found Paul and was not ashamed of his chains.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, an apostle by God’s will for the sake of the promise of life in Christ, writes to Timothy, his dear son, with grace, mercy and peace. This is his last letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his execution.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Personal Letter, Not a Church Order

There is no thanksgiving for a congregation because none is in view: this is an old man writing to a younger one while there is still time, and ‘mercy’ appears in the greeting as it does only in the letters to Timothy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul calls himself the Lord's prisoner, not Rome's (v.8; cf. Eph 3:1).

Now: A man facing execution opens his last letter with ‘the promise of the life’ — the letter's whole argument in its first sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

Meaning first. 2 Timothy 1 is a call not to be ashamed of the gospel, written by a man about to die for it. Paul is in prison again in Rome, this time with no expectation of release (4:6–8). After greeting Timothy warmly (vv. 1–2), he thanks God for him, remembers his tears, longs to see him, and recalls the sincere faith handed down through his grandmother and mother (vv. 3–5). Then he gets to the point: fan into flame God’s gift, because God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power, love and self-control; so do not be ashamed of the testimony about Christ or of Paul in chains, but share in suffering for the gospel (vv. 6–8). That gospel is then described in one of Scripture’s richest summaries: God saved and called us not by our works but by his own purpose and grace, given in Christ before time began, now revealed in Christ’s appearing, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light (vv. 9–10). Paul suffers for this gospel, yet is not ashamed, because he knows whom he has believed and that Christ will guard what Paul has entrusted to him (vv. 11–12). So Timothy must hold to the pattern of sound words and guard the good deposit by the Spirit (vv. 13–14). The chapter ends with two contrasting examples: all in Asia have turned away from Paul, but Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found him and was not ashamed of his chains (vv. 15–18).

Setting and background. This is Paul’s last surviving letter, written from prison in Rome around AD 64–67, probably during Nero’s persecution after the great fire of Rome (AD 64). His first imprisonment (Acts 28) had been a kind of house arrest with freedom to receive visitors; this one was harsher. He was chained like a criminal (1:16; 2:9), hard to find (1:17), and largely deserted (1:15; 4:10, 16). He had already had a first hearing (4:16) and expected execution. Tradition says he was beheaded on the road to Ostia. Timothy was still in Ephesus, or nearby, and Paul urged him to come quickly before winter (4:9, 21).

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God. Key words. “By the will of God”: Paul’s apostleship was God’s choice, not his own (1 Corinthians 1:1; Galatians 1:1, 15–16). Even in chains he remains God’s apostle.

According to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus. Key words. “According to” (kata, in keeping with, for the sake of). Paul was made an apostle to proclaim the promise of life. Facing death, he speaks of life. “The life that is in Christ Jesus”: eternal life, found only in union with him (John 11:25–26; 1 John 5:11–12).

To Timothy, my beloved child. Key words. “Beloved” (agapētō, dearly loved). In 1 Timothy 1:2, it was “true child”; here, more tenderly, “beloved child.” These are a dying father’s words.

Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. Key words. The same triple blessing as 1 Timothy 1:2. Grace for the undeserving, mercy for the suffering, peace for the troubled.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was bitter or defeated in prison. The letter is full of confidence in Christ. Nor is it merely a private note; though deeply personal, it is apostolic Scripture for the church (4:22 ends with “you” plural).

In a sentence. From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by God’s will, sent to proclaim the promised life that is found in Christ Jesus, to Timothy, my dearly loved son: grace, mercy and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.

On a Tuesday. When things are hard, remember the promise of life in Christ Jesus. Death is not the last word for those in him.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s last surviving letter, written from prison in Rome as he expected to die, probably in the mid 60s AD under Nero. Timothy was probably still in Ephesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–14 — Fan Into Flame, and Guard the Deposit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God, whom he serves with a clear conscience, and prays for Timothy constantly, remembering his tears at parting and longing to see him. He recalls Timothy’s sincere faith, first seen in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. So he urges him to rekindle God’s gift given through the laying on of Paul’s hands, for God gave a spirit not of fear but of power, love and self-control. Timothy must not be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul the prisoner, but share in suffering, relying on God, who saved and called us by his own purpose and grace, given in Christ before time began and now revealed in Christ, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light. For this gospel Paul suffers unashamed, sure that God will guard what he has entrusted. Timothy is to hold to the pattern of sound teaching and guard the good deposit by the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Deposits, Running Opposite Ways

Paul has entrusted his deposit to God, who is able to guard it (v.12); God has entrusted a deposit to Timothy, who must guard it by the indwelling Spirit (v.14). And behind both stands the grace given in Christ before the ages began, by the Saviour who abolished death (vv.9–10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The faith came to Timothy through his grandmother and mother (v.5; Acts 16:1), long before any laying on of hands.

Now: To a timid man Paul names what he has been given — power, love and a sound mind (v.7) — rather than telling him to feel braver.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience, as I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day. As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience, as I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day. As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.

I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors. Key words. “Serve” (latreuō, worship, serve in a religious sense). “Ancestors” (progonōn, forefathers). Paul sees continuity between the faith of Israel and his faith in Christ. He worships the same God as Abraham, Moses and David (Acts 24:14; 26:6–7). Christianity is not a new religion but the fulfilment of the old.

With a clear conscience. Key words. “Clear” (kathara, pure). Paul is not claiming sinlessness, but integrity: his conscience does not accuse him of hypocrisy in his ministry (Acts 23:1; 24:16). Even his persecution of the church had been done in ignorance and sincere zeal (1 Timothy 1:13), though it was terribly wrong.

As I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day. Key words. “Constantly” (adialeiptos, without ceasing). Even in prison, Paul prays. Night and day: in a dark cell, time blurred, but prayer continued.

As I remember your tears. Key words. Probably the tears when Paul and Timothy last parted (Acts 20:37 shows the Ephesian elders weeping at a parting). Timothy was a man of deep feeling. Tears are not a sign of weakness in the Bible (John 11:35; Romans 12:15).

I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy. Key words. “Long” (epipotheō, yearn intensely). Paul was lonely (4:9–11, 16). He wanted Timothy with him at the end.

What it does not mean. “As did my ancestors” does not mean all Jews of Paul’s time served God rightly; Paul knew that many did not (Romans 10:1–3). He means the true line of faith from Abraham, of which he is part. Nor does a clear conscience mean Paul thought himself righteous before God by his own works (Philippians 3:9).

In a sentence. I give thanks to God, whom I worship with a clean conscience as my forefathers did, as I keep remembering you in my prayers night and day. Remembering your tears, I long to see you, so that my joy may be complete.

On a Tuesday. Who do you remember in prayer “night and day”? Write a note or send a message to someone you love and miss.

verseByVerse.quote: I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.

I am reminded of your sincere faith. Key words. “Sincere” (anypokritou, unhypocritical, genuine), as in 1 Timothy 1:5. Timothy’s faith was real.

A faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice. Key words. “Dwelt” (enōkēsen, lived in, made its home in). Faith had made its home in three generations. Timothy’s father was a Greek, apparently not a believer (Acts 16:1); his faith came through his mother and grandmother, who were Jewish believers, likely converted on Paul’s first visit to Lystra (Acts 14:6–7). They had taught him the Scriptures from childhood (3:15), so that when the gospel came, he was ready.

And now, I am sure, dwells in you as well. Key words. “I am sure” (pepeismai, I have been persuaded). Faith is personal; it must dwell in each person. Grandmother’s and mother’s faith did not save Timothy, but God used them as means to bring him to his own faith.

Where Christians differ: are children of believers automatically in the covenant? Paedobaptists see verses like this as evidence of covenant continuity in families, supporting infant baptism. Verdict: This verse shows the great value of believing parents and grandparents, who teach their children the Scriptures from infancy. God often works through families. But faith is not inherited; each person must come to faith personally (John 1:12–13). Timothy was taught as a child, believed for himself, and was then baptised as a believer. Baptism belongs to those who profess faith. This is held charitably toward our paedobaptist brothers, who equally insist that each child must come to personal faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is passed on genetically or by family membership. It is God’s gift to each person (Ephesians 2:8). Nor does it mean children of unbelieving or absent fathers are at a disadvantage before God; Timothy is the proof.

In a sentence. I am reminded of your genuine faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice, and which I am convinced now lives in you too.

On a Tuesday. Parents and grandparents: read the Bible with your children and grandchildren. Single mothers: take heart from Eunice. And thank God for those who taught you the faith.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy’s father was a Greek; his faith came through his mother’s side.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.

For this reason I remind you. Key words. “For this reason”: because your faith is genuine (v. 5). Real faith can still burn low.

To fan into flame the gift of God. Key words. “Fan into flame” (anazōpyreō, rekindle, keep blazing, stir up the embers). Present tense: keep it burning. The image is of a fire that has died down to embers and needs to be fanned back to full flame. Timothy had not lost his gift, but under pressure and fear it was smouldering. “Gift” (charisma), as in 1 Timothy 4:14: his gift for ministry.

Which is in you through the laying on of my hands. Key words. Paul, together with the elders (1 Timothy 4:14), had laid hands on Timothy when he was set apart for ministry. The gift came from God; the laying on of hands marked and confirmed it.

For God gave us a spirit not of fear. Key words. “Fear” (deilias, cowardice, timidity). Timothy seems to have been naturally timid (1 Corinthians 16:10). “Spirit” may refer to the Holy Spirit (so “God gave us the Spirit, who is not a Spirit of fear”), or to a disposition God gives. Most likely the Holy Spirit, as in verse 14 and Romans 8:15, who produces these qualities in us.

But of power and love and self-control. Key words. “Power” (dynameōs, strength, ability), to endure and to speak boldly (Acts 1:8). “Love” (agapēs), for God and for people, which casts out fear (1 John 4:18). “Self-control” (sōphronismou, sound mind, discipline, sober judgement), the steadiness to think clearly under pressure. The Spirit does not remove our personality but strengthens it with his own qualities.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians will never feel fear. Paul himself felt it (1 Corinthians 2:3). It means fear does not have to rule us, because the Spirit gives power, love and a sound mind to act rightly despite it. Nor does it mean the gift works automatically; Timothy must stir it up.

In a sentence. That is why I remind you to keep fanning into a blaze the gift God gave you when I laid my hands on you. For the Spirit God has given us does not make us cowards; he gives power, love and a disciplined mind.

On a Tuesday. What has fear stopped you doing for Christ? Ask the Spirit for power, love and a clear head, and take one step this week.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God,

Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord. Key words. “Ashamed” (epaischynthēs, embarrassed by, disowning). A keyword of the chapter (vv. 8, 12, 16). “The testimony about our Lord”: the gospel, the witness to Christ crucified and risen. In the Roman world, the gospel of a crucified Jew was foolishness and scandal (1 Corinthians 1:23). Under Nero’s persecution, it was also dangerous. The temptation to be ashamed was real (Mark 8:38; Romans 1:16).

Nor of me his prisoner. Key words. “His prisoner”: not Nero’s prisoner, but Christ’s. Paul is in chains because of Christ, and under Christ’s sovereign control (Ephesians 3:1; 4:1; Philemon 1, 9). To associate with a condemned prisoner was dangerous and shameful in Roman eyes. Many had distanced themselves (v. 15).

But share in suffering for the gospel. Key words. “Share in suffering” (synkakopathēson, suffer evil together with, endure hardship alongside). A word Paul may have coined. Join me in suffering. Suffering for the gospel is a fellowship, shared with Paul and with Christ (Philippians 3:10; 1 Peter 4:13).

By the power of God. Key words. Not by our own strength. God gives the power to endure (v. 7; Colossians 1:11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should seek suffering, or that all suffering is for the gospel. It means we should not avoid the suffering that comes from faithfulness to Christ.

In a sentence. So do not be embarrassed to bear witness about our Lord, or embarrassed by me, his prisoner; instead, join with me in suffering for the gospel, relying on God’s power,

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to hide your faith? Name it, and ask God for the courage not to be ashamed.

verseByVerse.quote: who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began, and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began, and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel,

Who saved us. Key words. “Saved” (sōsantos, aorist: a completed act). The power that enables us to suffer is the power that saved us. Salvation is God’s work from first to last.

And called us to a holy calling. Key words. “Called” (kalesantos). God’s effectual call: the inward work of the Spirit, through the gospel, by which God brings his chosen ones to faith (Romans 8:30; 1 Corinthians 1:9). “Holy calling”: a calling to be holy, set apart for God (1 Thessalonians 4:7), and a calling that comes from a holy God.

Not because of our works. Key words. Salvation is not a reward for anything we have done, are doing, or will do (Ephesians 2:8–9; Titus 3:5). Not even foreseen works or foreseen faith.

But because of his own purpose and grace. Key words. “Purpose” (prothesin, plan, resolve, setting forth beforehand). “His own”: the reason for salvation lies entirely in God, not in us. “Grace” (charin, undeserved favour). God’s plan to save is a plan of pure grace.

Which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began. Key words. “Before the ages began” (pro chronōn aiōniōn, before eternal times, before time itself). Grace was given to us in Christ before we existed, before creation. This is election: God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4–5). Since it was given before we did anything, it cannot depend on anything we do.

And which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus. Key words. “Manifested” (phanerōtheisan, revealed, made visible). “Appearing” (epiphaneias), the same word used of his second coming (1 Timothy 6:14), here used of his first coming. What God planned in eternity he revealed in history, when Christ came.

Who abolished death. Key words. “Abolished” (katargēsantos, rendered powerless, made ineffective, put out of action). Christ has broken death’s power. It still happens, but it no longer has the last word, and its sting, sin, has been removed (1 Corinthians 15:54–57; Hebrews 2:14–15). For a man about to be executed, this was not theory.

And brought life and immortality to light through the gospel. Key words. “Brought to light” (phōtisantos, illuminated, revealed clearly). “Immortality” (aphtharsian, incorruptibility, imperishability). The Old Testament had glimpses of life beyond death (Job 19:25–27; Daniel 12:2), but in Christ’s resurrection it is revealed in full light. “Through the gospel”: the message that announces it.

Where Christians differ: is election based on foreseen faith? Arminians teach that God chose those whom he foresaw would believe. Verdict: This verse rules it out: God saved us not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, given before time began. If election were based on foreseen faith, it would be because of something in us. Faith is the result of God’s choice, not its cause (Acts 13:48; Ephesians 2:8). This is unconditional election, and it is the strongest ground of assurance: what God purposed before time, he will not abandon.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is unnecessary; God saves through faith, which he gives. Nor does “abolished death” mean believers will not die physically, unless Christ returns first. It means death is defeated and will finally be destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26).

In a sentence. who rescued us and called us to a holy life, not because of anything we had done, but because of his own plan and grace. He gave us this grace in Christ Jesus before time began, and has now revealed it through the coming of our Saviour, Christ Jesus, who broke the power of death and through the gospel brought life and immortality into the light,

For worship. Thank God that he chose you in Christ before time began, not for anything in you. Rest in that grace when you face death or fear.

verseByVerse.quote: for which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher, which is why I suffer as I do. But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher, which is why I suffer as I do. But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.

For which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher. Key words. “For which”: the gospel of verses 9–10. “Preacher” (kēryx, herald), “apostle” (apostolos, sent one), “teacher” (didaskalos). Three aspects of Paul’s calling: proclaiming, representing, explaining (1 Timothy 2:7).

Which is why I suffer as I do. Key words. Paul’s suffering is not because he has done wrong but because of his gospel ministry.

But I am not ashamed. Key words. Paul practises what he urged Timothy (v. 8).

For I know whom I have believed. Key words. “Know” (oida, know with settled certainty). “Whom”: not what, but whom. Paul’s confidence is in a person, Christ. “Have believed” (pepisteuka, perfect tense: I have trusted and keep trusting).

And I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me. Key words. “Convinced” (pepeismai, persuaded). “Able” (dynatos, powerful enough). “Guard” (phylaxai, keep safe). “That day”: the day of Christ’s return and judgement (1:18; 4:8). “What has been entrusted to me” (tēn parathēkēn mou, my deposit). The phrase can mean either what Paul has entrusted to Christ (his life, his soul, his salvation), or what Christ has entrusted to Paul (the gospel). Since verse 14 uses the same word for the gospel entrusted to Timothy, it may mean the gospel: Christ will guard his own message. But most take it as Paul’s life committed to Christ: Paul has deposited his soul with Christ, and Christ will keep it safe until the last day. Both are true.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s confidence was in the strength of his own faith. It was in the One he believed and in his power to keep. Nor does it mean Christ will spare Paul from death; Christ will keep him through death.

In a sentence. It is for this gospel that I was made a herald, an apostle and a teacher, and that is why I am suffering like this. Yet I am not ashamed, because I know the one I have trusted, and I am sure he is able to keep safe what I have placed in his hands until that day.

For worship. Entrust your life, your loved ones and your eternal future to Christ today. He is able to guard them.

verseByVerse.quote: Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.

Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me. Key words. “Follow” (eche, hold, keep). “Pattern” (hypotypōsin, outline, model, sketch, standard), as in 1 Timothy 1:16. The apostolic teaching provides a fixed framework. Timothy must not invent new doctrine but hold to the outline Paul gave him. “Sound” (hygiainontōn, healthy). “Heard from me”: oral teaching, now preserved in Scripture.

In the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. Key words. Not merely holding correct doctrine coldly, but with faith (trusting it) and love (gentleness toward others). Truth and love belong together (Ephesians 4:15).

By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us. Key words. “Dwells” (enoikountos, lives in, has his home in). The same word as verse 5: as faith dwelt in Lois, so the Spirit dwells in believers (Romans 8:9, 11). The task of guarding truth is impossible in human strength; the Spirit enables it.

Guard the good deposit entrusted to you. Key words. “Guard” (phylaxon), as in 1 Timothy 6:20. “Good deposit” (tēn kalēn parathēkēn): the gospel, the apostolic faith. Christ guards what Paul entrusted to him (v. 12); now Timothy, by the Spirit, must guard what has been entrusted to him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church may add new doctrines to the apostolic pattern. The deposit is complete; our task is to guard it, not expand it (Jude 3). Nor does guarding mean hiding; the gospel is guarded best by being faithfully taught.

In a sentence. Keep as your standard the healthy words you heard from me, holding them in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. With the help of the Holy Spirit who lives in us, guard the precious truth that has been placed in your care.

On a Tuesday. Is your church holding to the pattern of sound words? Pray for your teachers, and know the gospel well enough to recognise distortions.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul contrasts two kinds of friend. Everyone in the province of Asia has turned away from him, including Phygelus and Hermogenes. But Onesiphorus often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chains; in Rome he searched hard until he found Paul, as he had served him in Ephesus. Paul prays that the Lord will show mercy to his household and to him on that day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shame, and the Man Who Refused It

‘Ashamed’ runs through the chapter (vv.8, 12, 16). The turning away of verse 15 was most likely personal desertion of a dangerous prisoner rather than apostasy — a more ordinary failure, and a more likely one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Asia, the scene of Paul's most fruitful work (Acts 19:10), turned away at the end.

Now: Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found a condemned man (v.17) — an answer to shame available to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.

You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me. Key words. “Asia” was the Roman province in western Turkey whose chief city was Ephesus, where Timothy was. “Turned away” (apestraphēsan, deserted, repudiated). “All” is probably a sad generalisation, meaning a large number, or possibly those from Asia who had been in Rome and failed to stand by Paul at his trial (4:16). Under Nero’s persecution, association with a prisoner was dangerous. It does not necessarily mean they abandoned the faith, but that they abandoned Paul, perhaps out of fear.

Among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes. Key words. Otherwise unknown. Perhaps they had been prominent leaders whose desertion was especially painful. Their only memorial is this: they turned away.

What it does not mean. It does not mean literally every believer in Asia; Onesiphorus was from Ephesus (vv. 16–18), and Timothy himself was there. It is the language of grief.

In a sentence. You know that everyone in the province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes.

On a Tuesday. Who is suffering for Christ and feeling abandoned? Do not be the one who turns away. Call, visit, or write.
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province in western Turkey whose chief city was Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains, but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me— may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains, but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me— may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.

May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus. Key words. “Onesiphorus” means “profit-bringer” or “help-bringer.” He lived up to his name. Paul prays for his household, his family. Some believe Onesiphorus had died, since Paul prays for his household rather than for him directly, and greets his household in 4:19 without him.

For he often refreshed me. Key words. “Refreshed” (anepsyxen, revived, cooled, gave fresh air). His visits were like a breath of fresh air in a stifling prison.

And was not ashamed of my chains. Key words. The contrast with verse 15, and the model for Timothy (v. 8). He was willing to be associated with a condemned prisoner.

But when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me. Key words. “Searched earnestly” (spoudaiōs ezētēsen, sought diligently, eagerly). Paul was hard to find, perhaps in a dungeon. Onesiphorus persisted, at risk to himself, asking around in a hostile city until he found him.

May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day! Key words. A wordplay: he found Paul; may he find mercy. “That day”: the day of judgement (v. 12). The double “Lord” may refer to Christ granting mercy from the Father, or is simply emphatic.

And you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus. Key words. “Service” (diēkonēsen, ministered). He had a record of serving in Ephesus too.

Where Christians differ: does this verse support prayer for the dead? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse, if Onesiphorus had died, to support prayers for the dead and the doctrine of purgatory. Verdict: It is not certain that Onesiphorus had died; he may simply have been away from home. Even if he had, Paul’s words are a wish expressing his gratitude, not a prayer to change the condition of a soul. Scripture teaches that at death believers go immediately into the presence of Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43), and that our eternal state is settled at death (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27). There is no purgatory, for Christ’s sacrifice has fully paid for the sins of believers (Hebrews 10:14). We should not pray for the dead to be released from punishment, though we may thank God for them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Onesiphorus earned mercy by his service. Mercy is by definition undeserved. His service was the fruit of grace, and Paul prays that God would show him mercy on the last day.

In a sentence. May the Lord show mercy to the family of Onesiphorus, because he often revived my spirits and was not ashamed that I was in chains. When he came to Rome, he hunted hard for me until he found me. May the Lord grant that he finds mercy from the Lord on that day! And you know very well how much he did to help in Ephesus.

On a Tuesday. Be an Onesiphorus: seek out someone who is isolated or suffering, and refresh them.

But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.<sup>13</sup>Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.<sup>14</sup>By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.<sup>15</sup>You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.<sup>16</sup>May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains,<sup>17</sup>but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me—<sup>18</sup>may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.

2.title: Soldier, Athlete, Farmer: The Shape of Gospel Ministry
2.overview:
Paul tells Timothy what gospel ministry is like. Be strengthened by grace, and hand the teaching on to reliable people who will teach others. Endure like a soldier, train like an athlete, labour like a farmer. Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead: Paul is chained, but God’s word is not. A trustworthy saying holds it together: if we died with him we will live with him; if we are faithless, he remains faithful.

The second half turns to false teaching. Avoid word-fights, which ruin the listeners. Cut the word of truth straight. Hymenaeus and Philetus say the resurrection has already happened, but God’s foundation stands: “The Lord knows those who are his.” Cleanse yourself to be useful to the Master, run from youthful passions with others who seek God, and correct opponents gently, because repentance is God’s gift.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — A Good Soldier of Christ Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges Timothy to draw strength from the grace that is in Christ and to hand on the teaching he received to reliable people who will teach others in turn. He must be ready to suffer, like a soldier who stays free of civilian distractions to please his commander, an athlete who keeps the rules to win, and a farmer who works hard and so gets the first of the harvest. He is to keep Jesus Christ in mind, risen from the dead and descended from David, the gospel for which Paul is in chains like a criminal, though God’s message cannot be chained. Paul endures it all for the sake of God’s chosen people, that they too may be saved. A reliable saying sums it up: those who die with Christ will live with him, those who endure will reign with him, those who disown him will be disowned, but even when we are unfaithful he stays faithful, because he cannot be untrue to himself.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Broken Symmetry of Verse 13

The hymn's first three lines match our action with his response; the fourth breaks the pattern in our favour — we are faithless, he remains faithful — grounded not in our sincerity but in his nature: ‘he cannot deny himself’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: From a death cell Paul arranges for the deposit to pass through four generations of faithful men (v.2).

Now: Soldier, athlete, farmer (vv.3–6): singleness, discipline and patience — and the word of God is not bound (v.9).

verseByVerse.quote: You then, my child, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You then, my child, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.

Meaning first. 2 Timothy 2 tells Timothy how to persevere in ministry and how to deal with false teaching. It begins with strength from grace and a plan for the future: pass the apostolic teaching on to faithful men who will teach others (vv. 1–2). Then three pictures of the committed Christian worker: the soldier who avoids entanglements and aims to please his commander, the athlete who competes by the rules, and the hard-working farmer who earns the first share of the crop (vv. 3–7). The motive for such endurance is Christ himself, risen from the dead and descended from David, the gospel for which Paul is chained, though the word of God is not chained; Paul endures for the sake of God’s elect, so that they too may obtain salvation (vv. 8–10). A trustworthy saying, perhaps an early hymn, sets out what is at stake: dying and living with Christ, enduring and reigning with him, the danger of denying him, and his unchanging faithfulness (vv. 11–13). The second half turns to false teaching (vv. 14–26): Timothy must forbid quarrels about words, work hard to be an approved workman who handles the word of truth rightly, avoid empty chatter that spreads like gangrene (as in Hymenaeus and Philetus, who said the resurrection had already happened), and take comfort that God’s foundation stands firm. He must be a clean vessel, flee youthful passions, pursue righteousness, avoid foolish controversies, and correct opponents gently, in the hope that God will grant them repentance and rescue them from the devil’s trap.

You then, my child, be strengthened. Key words. “You then” (sy oun): in contrast with those who deserted Paul (1:15), and following the example of Onesiphorus (1:16–18). “Be strengthened” (endynamou, be empowered), present passive: keep on being made strong. The strength is received, not produced.

By the grace that is in Christ Jesus. Key words. Grace is not only the power that saves us at the beginning but the power that sustains us throughout (2 Corinthians 12:9). It is found “in Christ Jesus,” through union with him.

And what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses. Key words. The apostolic teaching, delivered publicly, confirmed by many who heard it. It was not secret knowledge, unlike the false teachers’ claims (1 Timothy 6:20). Its truth could be checked.

Entrust to faithful men. Key words. “Entrust” (parathou, commit as a deposit), from the same root as “deposit” (1:12, 14). “Faithful” (pistois, trustworthy, reliable). “Men” (anthrōpois, people; but in context, those who will teach in the church, the elders). Timothy must choose carefully who receives the deposit.

Who will be able to teach others also. Key words. “Able” (hikanoi, competent, qualified). Four generations are in view: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others. The gospel is to be handed on in an unbroken chain of faithful teaching. Every generation must train the next.

Where Christians differ: is this apostolic succession? Roman Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican traditions teach that the bishops form an unbroken line from the apostles, through which authority and grace are passed by ordination. Verdict: What is passed on here is the apostolic teaching, not an office or a sacramental power. True succession is succession in doctrine: those who faithfully teach what the apostles taught stand in the apostolic line. A man ordained in an unbroken line who teaches error is no successor of the apostles (Galatians 1:8–9). The apostolic deposit is now held in Scripture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only ordained leaders need to know the gospel. All believers should know it well. But the church must deliberately train teachers.

In a sentence. As for you, my son, keep drawing your strength from the grace that is in Christ Jesus. What you heard from me, confirmed by many witnesses, hand on to trustworthy people who will be competent to teach others too.

On a Tuesday. Who are you training to know and teach the faith? Think of one person you could invest in this year.

verseByVerse.quote: Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him.

Share in suffering. Key words. “Share in suffering” (synkakopathēson), the same word as 1:8. Suffering for the gospel is shared.

As a good soldier of Christ Jesus. Key words. “Soldier” (stratiōtēs). Roman soldiers endured hard training, long marches, poor food, and danger. The Christian worker must expect the same (Philippians 2:25; Philemon 2). “Good” (kalos, noble, fine).

No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits. Key words. “Entangled” (empleketai, woven into, caught up in, like a net). “Civilian pursuits” (tais tou biou pragmateiais, the affairs of everyday life, business). Roman soldiers on active service were forbidden to engage in trade or farming. They had to be ready to fight. The Christian worker must not become so absorbed in ordinary concerns that he neglects his calling.

Since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him. Key words. “Enlisted” (stratologēsanti, recruited, enrolled as a soldier). Christ enlisted us. Our aim is to please him, not ourselves or others (2 Corinthians 5:9; Galatians 1:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers may never work at a trade; Paul himself made tents (Acts 18:3). The point is not being entangled: allowing ordinary affairs to become a distraction from the main task. Nor does it make ordinary work unspiritual for other Christians.

In a sentence. Take your share of hardship like a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier on duty gets tangled up in everyday business, because he wants to please the officer who enlisted him.

On a Tuesday. What is entangling you, distracting you from Christ’s calling? Identify it and loosen its grip this week.

verseByVerse.quote: An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops. Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops. Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.

An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. Key words. “Athlete” (athlē, competes in games). “Crowned” (stephanoutai): victors in Greek games received a wreath (stephanos). “According to the rules” (nomimōs, lawfully). In the Olympic games, athletes swore to have trained for ten months and to follow the rules. Breaking them meant disqualification. In ministry, there are God’s rules: holiness, truth, endurance. No shortcuts.

It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops. Key words. “Hard-working” (kopiōnta, labouring to weariness). Farming involves long, slow, patient toil, with results that come only after waiting. But the farmer who works hard has the first right to the harvest. Ministry is similar: hard, often unseen, slow-growing work, but there will be fruit, and the worker will share in it, both in this life (1 Corinthians 9:7–11) and the next.

Think over what I say. Key words. “Think over” (noei, consider, reflect on, understand). Paul does not explain every detail of the pictures. Timothy must meditate on them.

For the Lord will give you understanding in everything. Key words. “Understanding” (synesin, insight, comprehension). Reflection and divine illumination work together. We think hard; God gives understanding (Proverbs 2:1–6; James 1:5).

What it does not mean. The athlete’s crown does not mean we earn salvation by keeping rules. The crown is the reward God graciously gives to faithful service (4:8; 1 Corinthians 9:25). Nor does the farmer’s share mean ministry is about financial gain.

In a sentence. An athlete wins the prize only if he competes by the rules. The farmer who has done the hard work should be the first to enjoy the harvest. Think about what I am saying, and the Lord will give you insight into all of it.

On a Tuesday. Your work for Christ may feel slow and unseen. Keep going: the harvest is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel, for which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel, for which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!

Remember Jesus Christ. Key words. “Remember” (mnēmoneue, keep in mind, keep remembering). Present tense: keep him in view. In hardship, the greatest encouragement is not a technique but a person.

Risen from the dead. Key words. “Risen” (egēgermenon, perfect participle: raised and still alive). He is not a dead hero but a living Lord. For a man facing execution, and for Timothy facing danger, the resurrection is everything. Death is not the end.

The offspring of David. Key words. “Offspring” (ek spermatos Dauid, of David’s seed). Christ is truly human and the promised Messianic King (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Romans 1:3–4). The resurrection proves he is the Son of God; his descent from David proves he is the promised King and truly human. Both together form the heart of the gospel. This also counters the false teachers who perhaps downplayed his true humanity.

As preached in my gospel. Key words. Not that it belongs to Paul, but the gospel Paul preaches (Romans 2:16; 16:25).

For which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. Key words. “Criminal” (kakourgos, evildoer), the word used of the criminals crucified with Jesus (Luke 23:32–33). Paul is treated like a common criminal, not merely a political prisoner.

But the word of God is not bound! Key words. “Bound” (dedetai, chained). Paul is chained; the gospel is not. It goes on spreading through others, through Paul’s letters, through those who visit him (Philippians 1:12–14). No prison can hold God’s word (Isaiah 55:11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s suffering was pointless or that God was absent. God was working through it.

In a sentence. Keep remembering Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, a descendant of David: that is my gospel, and for it I am suffering, even being chained like a criminal. But God’s word is not in chains!

For worship. Remember Jesus Christ today: risen, alive, reigning. Let that truth carry you through whatever is pressing on you.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.

Therefore I endure everything. Key words. “Therefore”: because the word is not bound, Paul’s suffering is worth it. “Endure” (hypomenō, bear up under, remain steadfast). “Everything”: chains, loneliness, cold (4:13), betrayal, approaching death.

For the sake of the elect. Key words. “The elect” (tous eklektous, the chosen ones). Those whom God chose before time began (1:9; Ephesians 1:4). This includes those already converted and those not yet converted, whom God will call through the gospel. Paul does not know who they are, but he knows they exist, and that gives him confidence that his suffering will not be in vain (Acts 18:10).

That they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus. Key words. “Obtain” (tychōsin, attain, reach, gain). Election does not make the gospel unnecessary. God’s chosen people come to salvation through the preaching of the gospel and the endurance of those who preach it. God ordains both the end (salvation) and the means (preaching, suffering, prayer).

With eternal glory. Key words. Salvation includes final glory: sharing in Christ’s glory forever (Romans 8:17–18, 30; 2 Corinthians 4:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean election makes evangelism pointless. Election is the reason evangelism will succeed. Nor does it mean Paul’s suffering atones for anyone; Christ alone saves. Paul’s suffering is the cost of bringing the message.

In a sentence. That is why I put up with everything for the sake of God’s chosen people, so that they too may receive the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, together with eternal glory.

On a Tuesday. Share the gospel with confidence: God has chosen people who will respond. Your effort is never in vain.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy, for: If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful— for he cannot deny himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy, for: If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful— for he cannot deny himself.

The saying is trustworthy. Key words. The fourth of the five trustworthy sayings (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; Titus 3:8). It is set out in four balanced lines, perhaps an early hymn sung in worship, or a baptismal confession.

If we have died with him, we will also live with him. Key words. “Died with” (synapethanomen, aorist: died together with, at a point in the past). This refers to our union with Christ in his death, which happens when we come to faith and is signified in baptism (Romans 6:3–8; Colossians 3:3). It may also include martyrdom. Those who have died with Christ will live with him, now in new life and forever in resurrection.

If we endure, we will also reign with him. Key words. “Endure” (hypomenomen, present tense: keep on enduring). Perseverance under suffering. “Reign with him” (symbasileusomen). Those who suffer with Christ will share his kingdom (Romans 8:17; Revelation 3:21; 20:4–6).

If we deny him, he also will deny us. Key words. “Deny” (arnēsometha, disown, reject, renounce). Not a temporary failure under pressure, as with Peter (who repented), but a settled, final rejection of Christ. Jesus said: whoever denies me before men, I will deny before my Father (Matthew 10:33). This is a solemn warning. Those who finally reject Christ will be rejected by him.

If we are faithless, he remains faithful. Key words. “Faithless” (apistoumen, unfaithful, lacking faith). This line breaks the pattern: we might expect “he will be faithless to us,” but instead, “he remains faithful.” Our weakness, wavering, and failures do not change his faithfulness to his promises and his people.

For he cannot deny himself. Key words. Christ’s faithfulness is rooted in his own character. To abandon his people or break his promises would be to deny himself, to act contrary to his nature. This is impossible (Numbers 23:19; Titus 1:2; Hebrews 6:18).

Where Christians differ: if Christ remains faithful, can a believer still be denied? Some take the third and fourth lines as contradictory: either believers can be lost (line three), or not (line four). Others take the fourth line as a threat: he remains faithful to his warnings and will judge the faithless. Verdict: Line three describes final, deliberate apostasy, which reveals that a person never truly belonged to Christ (1 John 2:19); such people will be disowned. Line four describes the weakness of genuine believers, who sometimes falter, doubt or fail, like Peter. Christ’s faithfulness to them does not depend on their strength; he keeps them, and so they do not finally deny him (John 10:28–29; Luke 22:31–32). The warning is real, and it is one of the means by which Christ keeps his people from apostasy; the comfort is real, and it is the ground of their perseverance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean any momentary failure or doubt brings condemnation. Peter denied Christ three times and was restored (John 21:15–19). Nor does it mean Christ is indifferent to unfaithfulness; he disciplines his own (Hebrews 12:5–11).

In a sentence. Here is a saying you can rely on: if we died with him, we shall also live with him; if we keep enduring, we shall also reign with him; if we disown him, he too will disown us; if we are unfaithful, he stays faithful, because he cannot be untrue to himself.

For worship. Thank Christ that his faithfulness is greater than your weakness. And ask him to keep you from ever denying him.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth of the “trustworthy sayings,” perhaps an early hymn.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–26 — A Worker Approved by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy must keep warning the church, before God, against quarrelling over words, which ruins those who listen. He should work to be a worker God approves, unashamed, teaching the message of truth accurately, and avoid empty, irreverent talk, which spreads like an infection; Hymenaeus and Philetus, for instance, are upsetting people’s faith by claiming the resurrection has already happened. Still, God’s foundation stands firm, sealed with two truths: the Lord knows his own, and those who call on his name must turn from evil. Like household utensils, people can be fit for honourable use if they cleanse themselves. Timothy should run from youthful desires and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace with sincere believers, and refuse foolish arguments. The Lord’s servant must not fight but be kind, able to teach and patient, gently correcting opponents in the hope that God will grant them repentance and they will escape the devil’s snare.
verseByVerse.theology:
Cutting Straight

‘Rightly handling’ (v.15) is to cut straight, like a craftsman whose cut cannot be undone: accuracy, not eloquence. And God's foundation bears two seals (v.19) — the Lord knows his own, and those who name him depart from iniquity.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hymenaeus, already disciplined (1 Tim 1:20), was still teaching that the resurrection had come — wrecking the hope of the grieving first.

Now: Word-fights damage the hearers (v.14); cleanse yourself rather than audit the house (v.21); and correct with gentleness, since repentance is God's to grant (v.25).

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them of these things, and charge them before God not to quarrel about words, which does no good, but only ruins the hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remind them of these things, and charge them before God not to quarrel about words, which does no good, but only ruins the hearers.

Remind them of these things. Key words. “Remind” (hypomimnēske, keep reminding). “Them”: the faithful men (v. 2) and the church. “These things”: the truths of verses 1–13. Much of ministry is reminding people of what they already know (2 Peter 1:12–13).

And charge them before God. Key words. “Charge” (diamartyromenos, solemnly warn, testify earnestly). Before God, who sees and judges.

Not to quarrel about words. Key words. “Quarrel about words” (logomachein, fight with words, battle over terms), as in 1 Timothy 6:4. Arguments over trivial distinctions, word games, and speculative points.

Which does no good, but only ruins the hearers. Key words. “Does no good” (ep’ ouden chrēsimon, useful for nothing). “Ruins” (katastrophē, overthrows, upsets; our word “catastrophe”). Such quarrels do not merely waste time; they damage faith. Those listening are unsettled, confused, and led away from the truth.

What it does not mean. It does not mean words do not matter or that doctrine is unimportant. Precise words matter greatly (v. 15). The problem is quarrelling over words in a way that serves pride and controversy rather than truth.

In a sentence. Keep reminding people of these things, and warn them solemnly before God not to fight over words. It does no good and only wrecks the faith of those who listen.

On a Tuesday. Before you join an online theological argument, ask: will this build up or tear down those who are listening?

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.

Do your best. Key words. “Do your best” (spoudason, be eager, make every effort, be diligent). The KJV renders it “study.” Ministry of the Word requires hard work.

To present yourself to God as one approved. Key words. “Present” (parastēsai, stand before, offer). “To God”: the audience is God, not people. “Approved” (dokimon, tested and found genuine, like metal assayed and passed as pure). Timothy must seek God’s approval, not the crowd’s.

A worker who has no need to be ashamed. Key words. “Worker” (ergatēn, labourer, workman). Ministry is a craft. “No need to be ashamed” (anepaischynton, not put to shame): a workman whose work, when inspected, holds up.

Rightly handling the word of truth. Key words. “Rightly handling” (orthotomounta, cutting straight). The word was used of a road builder cutting a straight path, of a farmer ploughing a straight furrow, of a tentmaker (Paul’s trade) cutting leather in a straight line, or of a priest dividing a sacrifice. The idea is accuracy: handling God’s Word precisely, interpreting it correctly, teaching it faithfully, so that people are led straight. “The word of truth”: the gospel and the whole of Scripture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only scholars can understand Scripture; its main message is clear to all (Psalm 19:7). Nor does “rightly dividing” (KJV) mean dividing Scripture into separate dispensations with different ways of salvation, as some have taught. It means accurate handling of the whole Word.

In a sentence. Make every effort to stand before God as someone tested and approved, a workman with nothing to be ashamed of, who handles the message of truth accurately.

On a Tuesday. When you read Scripture, read it carefully: in context, asking what it meant, then what it means. Ask God to make you an accurate handler of his Word.

verseByVerse.quote: But avoid irreverent babble, for it will lead people into more and more ungodliness, and their talk will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have swerved from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened. They are upsetting the faith of some.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But avoid irreverent babble, for it will lead people into more and more ungodliness, and their talk will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have swerved from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened. They are upsetting the faith of some.

But avoid irreverent babble. Key words. “Avoid” (periistaso, go around, shun, stand clear of). “Irreverent babble” (bebēlous kenophōnias, godless empty chatter), as in 1 Timothy 6:20.

For it will lead people into more and more ungodliness. Key words. “Lead into more and more” (prokopsousin, advance, progress). Ironic: the false teachers claimed to be making spiritual progress; they were progressing, but into ungodliness. False doctrine never stands still; it gets worse.

And their talk will spread like gangrene. Key words. “Gangrene” (gangraina, a spreading, eating ulcer, cancer). Dead tissue that spreads and destroys healthy flesh. The contrast with “sound” (healthy) doctrine is vivid. False teaching is a disease that infects and kills.

Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus. Key words. Hymenaeus was named in 1 Timothy 1:20 as handed over to Satan. Apparently he had not repented. Philetus is otherwise unknown.

Who have swerved from the truth. Key words. “Swerved” (ēstochēsan, missed the mark), as in 1 Timothy 1:6 and 6:21.

Saying that the resurrection has already happened. Key words. They taught that the resurrection was purely spiritual, already experienced at conversion or baptism, so that there would be no future bodily resurrection. This probably came from a view that the body is unimportant or evil (1 Timothy 4:3). Paul had dealt with denial of the resurrection in Corinth (1 Corinthians 15:12). It is a serious error: without a bodily resurrection, Christianity is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:14–19).

They are upsetting the faith of some. Key words. “Upsetting” (anatrepousin, overturning, subverting, as one overturns a table). Real damage was being done.

What it does not mean. It does not deny that believers have already been raised with Christ spiritually (Ephesians 2:6; Colossians 3:1). That is true. The error is saying that is all there is, denying the future bodily resurrection.

In a sentence. But steer clear of godless, empty talk, because those who indulge in it will go further and further into ungodliness, and their teaching will spread like an eating sore. Hymenaeus and Philetus are among them; they have missed the truth by claiming that the resurrection has already taken place, and they are overturning some people’s faith.

For worship. Praise God for the hope of the bodily resurrection: you will be raised, body and soul, to be with Christ forever.

verseByVerse.quote: But God's firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: "The Lord knows those who are his," and, "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and, “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.”

But God’s firm foundation stands. Key words. “Firm” (stereos, solid, steadfast). “Foundation” (themelios). False teachers may overturn some people’s faith (v. 18), but they cannot overturn God’s foundation. The foundation is probably God’s church built on his truth (1 Timothy 3:15), or God’s saving work itself. “Stands” (hestēken, perfect tense: has stood and continues standing).

Bearing this seal. Key words. “Seal” (sphragis). In the ancient world, a foundation stone might bear an inscription indicating ownership and purpose. A seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity. God’s foundation has two inscriptions.

The Lord knows those who are his. Key words. The first inscription echoes the words Moses spoke during the rebellion of Korah, when God showed who truly belonged to him and who did not (Numbers 16:5). “Knows” (egnō) means more than awareness; it is God’s loving, electing knowledge, by which he chose and owns his people (John 10:14, 27; Romans 8:29; Galatians 4:9). When some fall away, the truly chosen remain, because God knows them. This is God’s side: his sovereign choice and keeping.

Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity. Key words. The second inscription perhaps echoes the warning in the same story, to depart from the tents of the wicked men (Numbers 16:26), and Isaiah 52:11. “Names the name of the Lord”: professes faith in Christ, calls on him. “Depart” (apostētō, withdraw, turn away). “Iniquity” (adikias, unrighteousness). This is our side: the evidence of belonging to God is turning from sin. Those who truly belong to the Lord will depart from evil.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s knowledge makes our holiness unnecessary. The two seals go together: God knows his own, and his own depart from iniquity. Election and holiness are inseparable (Ephesians 1:4; 2 Peter 1:10). Nor does it mean we can know infallibly who the elect are; we see the fruit.

In a sentence. Yet God’s solid foundation stands firm, stamped with these words: “The Lord knows those who belong to him,” and, “Everyone who calls on the Lord’s name must turn away from wickedness.”

For worship. When others fall away, take comfort: the Lord knows those who are his. And respond to his love by turning from sin today.
verseByVerse.note: The first saying echoes the rebellion of Korah; the second gathers the sense of Moses’ warning to leave the rebels’ tents.

parallels.desc: the LORD will show who is his
Depart, please, from the tents of these wicked men

verseByVerse.quote: Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use, some for dishonorable. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use, some for dishonorable. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work.

Now in a great house. Key words. “Great house” (megalē oikia, large household, mansion). The visible church, the household of God (1 Timothy 3:15), contains a mix of people.

There are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay. Key words. “Vessels” (skeuē, utensils, containers, dishes). A wealthy household had fine silver and gold dishes for banquets, and wooden or clay pots for rubbish and waste.

Some for honorable use, some for dishonorable. Key words. “Honorable” (timēn): used at the master’s table. “Dishonorable” (atimian): used for menial or disgusting tasks. In context, the dishonourable vessels are the false teachers like Hymenaeus and Philetus; the honourable are faithful believers.

Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable. Key words. “Cleanses himself” (ekkathērē heauton, purges himself thoroughly). “What is dishonorable” (apo toutōn, from these): from the false teachers and their teaching, and from the sin that goes with it. Separation from false teaching and sinful practice.

He will be a vessel for honorable use. Key words. The metaphor shifts: a person can choose to become an honourable vessel by cleansing himself.

Set apart as holy. Key words. “Set apart as holy” (hēgiasmenon, sanctified, perfect tense: having been set apart and remaining so). Consecrated for God’s use.

Useful to the master of the house. Key words. “Useful” (euchrēston, serviceable, profitable). “Master” (despotē). The aim is to be useful to Christ.

Ready for every good work. Key words. “Ready” (hētoimasmenon, prepared). Available and equipped for whatever service the master requires (3:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we save ourselves by cleansing ourselves; we are washed by Christ (1 Corinthians 6:11). It means believers, enabled by grace, must actively separate from error and sin in order to be fit for service (Philippians 2:12–13). Nor does it mean the church can ever be perfectly pure in this age; there will always be a mix (Matthew 13:24–30).

In a sentence. In a large house there are not only gold and silver dishes but also wooden and earthenware ones, some for special occasions and some for menial use. So if anyone keeps himself clean from what is dishonourable, he will be a vessel for special use, set apart, useful to the master, and ready for every good task.

On a Tuesday. What do you need to cleanse yourself from to be more useful to Christ? Confess it and turn from it today.

verseByVerse.quote: So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.

So flee youthful passions. Key words. “Flee” (pheuge, run from), as in 1 Timothy 6:11. “Youthful passions” (neōterikas epithymias, desires typical of youth). Not only sexual desire, though that is included, but also impatience, love of argument, self-assertion, pride, ambition, the desire for novelty, and hot-headedness, the kinds of passions to which young men are especially prone, and which feed the controversies Paul has been warning about. Timothy was perhaps in his thirties.

And pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace. Key words. “Pursue” (diōke, chase). Four virtues: “righteousness” (right living), “faith” (trust and faithfulness), “love,” and “peace” (harmony, the opposite of the quarrels in vv. 14, 23).

Along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart. Key words. “Call on the Lord” (epikaloumenōn ton kyrion): genuine believers who worship and pray to Christ (Romans 10:13; 1 Corinthians 1:2). “From a pure heart” (1 Timothy 1:5): sincere, not hypocritical. Timothy is not to pursue holiness alone, but in fellowship with other genuine believers. Separation from false teachers (v. 21) goes together with fellowship with true believers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean youth is sinful or that young people cannot be godly; Timothy himself was an example (1 Timothy 4:12). Nor does it mean we pursue holiness in isolation.

In a sentence. So run from the desires that drive the young, and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, together with all who call on the Lord with a clean heart.

On a Tuesday. Who are you pursuing godliness with? Find one or two believers to pray with and encourage regularly.

verseByVerse.quote: Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels. And the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels. And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.

Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies. Key words. “Have nothing to do with” (paraitou, refuse, decline). “Foolish” (mōras, stupid; our word “moron”). “Ignorant” (apaideutous, uneducated, undisciplined, ill-informed). “Controversies” (zētēseis, speculative questions).

You know that they breed quarrels. Key words. “Breed” (gennōsin, give birth to). “Quarrels” (machas, fights, battles).

And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome. Key words. “The Lord’s servant” (doulon kyriou, the Lord’s slave). A title used of Moses, David, and the prophets, here for Timothy and every minister. “Must not be quarrelsome” (ou dei machesthai, must not fight).

But kind to everyone. Key words. “Kind” (ēpion, gentle, mild), the word used of a nursing mother (1 Thessalonians 2:7). To everyone, including opponents.

Able to teach. Key words. “Able to teach” (didaktikon), as in 1 Timothy 3:2. The answer to error is not fighting but teaching.

Patiently enduring evil. Key words. “Patiently enduring evil” (anexikakon, bearing wrong without resentment, tolerant of wrongs). Taking hostility without retaliating.

Correcting his opponents with gentleness. Key words. “Correcting” (paideuonta, instructing, training, disciplining). “Opponents” (antidiatithemenous, those who set themselves against, who oppose). “Gentleness” (prautēti, meekness, humility, mildness). Not harshly, sarcastically or arrogantly.

God may perhaps grant them repentance. Key words. “Grant” (dōē, give). Repentance is God’s gift (Acts 5:31; 11:18). We cannot argue anyone into the kingdom. Our task is to teach patiently and gently; God’s is to change hearts. “Perhaps” (mēpote): we do not know whom God will grant repentance to, but we hope and pray.

Leading to a knowledge of the truth. Key words. “Knowledge” (epignōsin, full knowledge). Repentance and right belief go together (3:7; 1 Timothy 2:4).

And they may come to their senses. Key words. “Come to their senses” (ananēpsōsin, become sober again, wake up from drunkenness). False teaching is like intoxication; it clouds the mind.

And escape from the snare of the devil. Key words. “Escape” (ek, out of). “Snare” (pagidos, trap). The devil has trapped them.

After being captured by him to do his will. Key words. “Captured” (ezōgrēmenoi, taken alive, captured as prisoners of war). They are prisoners of the devil, doing his will without realising it. Grammatically, “his will” could refer to the devil’s will or God’s will; most take it as the devil’s.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers should never be firm or never confront error. Paul is firm throughout. It means confrontation is done with gentleness, patience and hope. Nor does “God may grant repentance” mean human response is not real; people do repent, but they repent because God grants it.

In a sentence. Refuse to get involved in foolish and ill-informed arguments; you know they only produce fights. The Lord’s servant must not be a fighter but must be gentle with everyone, able to teach, patient when wronged, correcting those who oppose him with humility. Perhaps God will give them repentance so that they come to know the truth, and they will come to their senses and get free from the devil’s trap, where he has held them captive to do his will.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone who opposes the truth. Pray for God to grant them repentance, and speak to them gently next time you have the chance.
